2020/7.approach: A Parsec parser reads the rules; part 1 inverts them into a contained-by map and runs a Seq-queue BFS from shiny gold, part 2 recursively sums quantities over the forward map.
2020/7.critique: Inverting the map turns part 1 into plain reachability. The BFS never checks `seen` before enqueuing, so colours reached by several paths are expanded repeatedly, and `countBagsInside` is not memoised. `satisfy isDigit` assumes single-digit quantities. On a parse error `readRules` prints it and returns an empty rule list, so the parts silently produce a count rather than failing.

2020/8.approach: Parses instructions with Parsec into a Vector, steps a small machine inside the State monad while tracking visited counters in a Set, and brute-forces part 2 by trying every single jmp/nop swap.
2020/8.critique: Newtypes for Counter and Accumulator plus a pure stepMachine keep the interpreter readable, and laziness means head stops at the first terminating variant. Each candidate copies the whole vector with V.// and reruns from scratch, giving O(n²) work. The opcode case, sign case, irrefutable Jmp/Nop patterns and Right-only parse match are partial, and a jump landing past the end without equalling the length would crash at V.!.

2020/9.approach: Part 1 slides a 25-element window and checks each next number against a Set of the window for a pair sum; part 2 tries each start index and extends rightward until the running sum reaches or exceeds the target.
2020/9.critique: `canSum` rebuilds `S.fromList preamble` for every `p` instead of once per window. Part 2 restarts the scan at every start index rather than keeping a running two-pointer window, so its cost depends on how quickly sums overshoot. It fails at runtime if the input runs out before an invalid number, `head` finds no range, or `V.!` indexes past the end. part2 rereads the input through part1.

2020/10.approach: Sorts the joltages. Part 1 counts gaps of one and three in one pass. Part 2 memoises a keep-or-skip recursion over (previous joltage, remaining list) using monad-memo.
2020/10.critique: The keep/skip recursion encodes each adapter choice directly, and `threes + 1` accounts for the device's final gap. Memo keys hold whole list suffixes, so each Map lookup compares lists rather than an index. Part 1 calls `error` on any gap other than 1 or 3, and the parameter name `last` shadows Prelude.

2020/11.approach: Iterates a seating step on a Map grid to a fixed point through a pluggable adjacency function. Part 2 precomputes, per cell, the first non-floor seat along eight rays built by zipping coordinate ranges.
2020/11.critique: One fixGrid serves both parts via AdjacencyFn. `zip <$> [...] <*> [...]` pairs three x-sequences with three y-sequences, all eight directions after `drop 1`, and zip truncation stops rays at the border. Weaknesses: hard-coded width/height, non-exhaustive fromChar and case expressions that crash on unexpected input, and full Map rebuilds each step.

2020/12.approach: Parses actions with Parsec, then folds them over a ship state via an Actionable type class: a heading-plus-position Ship for part 1 and a ShipWaypoint with relative waypoint for part 2.
2020/12.critique: A shared `solve` fold over two Actionable/Manhattanable instances keeps both parts uniform; waypoint rotation is a coordinate swap with negation. Partial: `turn` and `rotate` (only 90/180/270), `opposite` (no F), `leftOf`/`rightOf`, `dirFromChar`, and the `Right` pattern. Its `line` parser demands '\n' after every action, so a file without a final newline fails. Dir mixes headings and turn commands.

2020/13.approach: Part 1 computes each bus's wait as busId - ts `rem` busId and takes the minimum. Part 2 filters out `BusX`, then folds `findNext` over the indexed bus IDs.
2020/13.critique: `findNext` advances `current` by `step` until `(current + offset) mod busId == 0`, then sets `step` to `step * busId`, so each search only scans multiples of the accumulated step. It has no `BusX` clause and relies on the earlier filter. Part 1 reports a wait of busId rather than 0 when ts is divisible by an ID. `readInput` uses a partial list pattern and `read`.

2020/14.approach: Parses instructions with Parsec into a typed AST, then runs them recursively through a Machine holding a Map from address to 36-bit lists; part 2 expands floating bits applicatively into all concrete addresses.
2020/14.critique: Explicit bit types (MaskBit, ValueBit) and the MemUpdater function parameter let both parts share one runMachine. maskBitFromChar and valueBitFromChar are partial, and `fromRight []` discards parse errors, leaving an empty instruction list instead of a reported failure. Values are stored as bit lists built through printf, which is wasteful. Part 2 enumerates 2^X addresses per write, workable only while masks have few Xs.

2020/15.approach: Simulates the game turn by turn, keeping a strict Data.Map from each spoken number to a list of its last one or two turns, and iterates `stepGame` until the target turn.
2020/15.critique: The state type and `stepUntil` loop read clearly, and `Strict` avoids thunk buildup over 30 million turns. Both `case` expressions are partial (no `Nothing` arm in the first, no `Just []` in the second), relying on invariants instead of types. Each turn does a few Map lookups and inserts, O(t log m) with heavy allocation where an unboxed mutable array would be far faster; the input is hard-coded.

2020/16.approach: A Parsec parser reads rules and tickets. Part 1 sums invalid values from nearby tickets only. Part 2 transposes valid tickets into columns and backtracks, caching failed remaining-rule sets in an IORef.
2020/16.critique: The dead-end cache is keyed on the remaining Set of Constraints, which implies the column position, so each failing subset is explored once, though distinct subsets can still number exponentially. `traverse` in IO explores every candidate branch even after one succeeds, and an IORef replaces pure state. `Right i` and `Just` are partial pattern matches.

2020/17.approach: Active cubes are kept as a sparse Data.Set of 4-tuples, with a Dim flag fixing w at 0 for part 1. Each of six steps re-evaluates every neighbour of an active cell.
2020/17.critique: One 4D coordinate type and a dimension switch inside `neighbours` let both parts share all the code, and the sparse set needs no bounds handling. The weak spot is `nub` for deduplicating candidates, which is quadratic. Collecting them into a Set would avoid that. The puzzle input is embedded via a quasiquote and the six steps are hard-coded.

2020/18.approach: Part 1 reverses each line and parses it with a right-recursive Parsec grammar, so right-associative parsing of the reversed text gives left-to-right evaluation. Part 2 rewrites operators and evaluates lines through Hint.
2020/18.critique: Reversing the string so naive right recursion acts like a left fold is compact, and the flipped parentheses are commented. Part 2 rewrites + and * to +: and *: and interprets each line with the Hint GHC interpreter. Those operators live in HintMixins.hs, which is not shown, so the precedence logic is not visible here. Operands go through digitToInt, so only single-digit numbers are supported.

2020/19.approach: Part 1 expands rule 0 into every string it generates and checks messages against a Set. Part 2 builds a Parsec parser accepting one or more rule-42 strings, then rule-31 strings, with more 42s than 31s.
2020/19.critique: Part 2 implements rules 0, 8 and 11 by hand as 42^n 31^m with n > m, so it depends on the input's rule 0 being "8 11". Its greedy many1 loops are correct only because rules 42 and 31 match disjoint fixed-length blocks. Enumerating every string for rules 0, 42 and 31 is exponential in grammar depth, and matches has no Nothing case, so a missing rule crashes.

2020/20.approach: Backtracking fills the square row-major: cell (0,0) tries every variant of every tile, later cells take unused variants matching neighbours' edges via precomputed edge-string maps; part 2 stitches border-stripped tiles and scans orientations for monsters.
2020/20.critique: Indexing every variant by left and top edge turns each later placement into a map lookup. The first cell tries every stored variant of every tile, `intersect` on lists is quadratic, and tile size 10 is hard-coded in the edge functions and chopBorders. solveJigsaw runs once per part, and `head`/`M.!` are partial.

2020/21.approach: Parses foods with Parsec, then backtracks over ingredients in the list monad, giving each an unused allergen or none in an allergen-to-ingredient map. Branches are pruned when a food's mapped allergen lacks its ingredient.
2020/21.critique: The `with ++ without` backtracking is short, and laziness lets `head` take the first complete mapping. It skips set intersection and elimination and rechecks every food at each node. `head` is partial, and the parser needs a trailing newline. `findValidMappings` declares `Map Ingredient Allergen` but builds allergen-keyed maps; it type-checks only because both aliases are `String`.

2020/22.approach: Both parts simulate the game on Data.Sequence decks. Part 2 recurses into sub-games on SQ.take prefixes and keeps a Set of seen (hand, hand) pairs, awarding player one on a repeat.
2020/22.critique: Matching the front with the :<| and Empty pattern synonyms and appending winners with >< keeps play and playRec close to the rules. The guards have no case for equal cards, and readInput's `let [h1, h2]` fails at runtime unless there are exactly two blocks. The seen-set stores whole Seq pairs compared structurally, so memory and comparison cost grow with game length.

2020/23.approach: Represents the cup circle as a successor map (IntMap from cup to next cup) and runs each move inside the State monad, splicing three cups out and back in with constant-count map updates.
2020/23.critique: The successor-map encoding makes each move a fixed number of lookups and inserts, so part 2's ten million moves finish without list rotation. IntMap still costs O(log n) per access, and the lazy State with `modify` can pile up thunks; an unboxed mutable array in ST would be much faster. `readOut` recomputes `length sofar` on every step, which is quadratic, though only nine cups are read. The puzzle input is hard-coded in the source.

2020/24.approach: Parses each path into hex directions, folds them with foldl' onto doubled-width coordinates to toggle a Set of black tiles, then runs 100 rounds of a Set-based cellular automaton over black tiles and their neighbours.
2020/24.critique: Doubled-width coordinates (E/W move x by 2) give integer hex positions without cube coordinates, and storing only black tiles in a Set limits each step to the live region. Each neighbour count builds a fresh six-element Set and intersects it with the whole black set, rather than counting membership directly. fromString is partial, and the parser's try/choice ordering is verbose.

2020/25.approach: Recovers one loop size by brute-force discrete logarithm, multiplying 7 repeatedly modulo 20201227 until it matches a public key, then applies that many modular multiplications to the other key.
2020/25.critique: The two `go` loops are short and easy to follow. `getLoopSize` is linear in the discovered loop size and `transform` is linear in its exponent argument, where square-and-multiply would be logarithmic. Both public keys are literals in this module, 7 and 20201227 recur as magic numbers, and `getLoopSize` never terminates if the target is unreachable.

2021/1.approach: Input is embedded at compile time via Template Haskell and parsed with decimal; numIncreasing zips `drop 1 xs` with `xs` into (next, current) pairs and counts those where fst > snd; part 2 first sums batch3 triples.
2021/1.critique: The reader-applicative predicate `(>) <$> fst <*> snd` keeps numIncreasing short, and part 2 reuses it unchanged after `batch3` and `fmap sum`. Summing each three-element window is more work than comparing values three apart, since shared terms cancel. readAs calls error on bad lines, and the embedded input fixes answers at compile time.

2021/2.approach: Parses each line with a Parsec `choice` into a Movement ADT, then runs a strict left fold of a part-specific step function over a three-field Submarine (x, depth, aim) and multiplies x by depth.
2021/2.critique: Sharing one `solve` and swapping only the step function keeps the two parts small, and the ADT makes each command explicit. Part 1 carries an unused aim field. Errors are handled with `error`: a bad line aborts in `parseWith`, and `number` uses the unsafe `read`. The input is embedded at compile time, so the module cannot run on a different file without recompiling.

2021/3.approach: Parses lines into [Bool] lists. Part 1 transposes them into columns and takes the majority bit per column; part 2 repeatedly filters rows by the common bit at an increasing index until one row remains.
2021/3.critique: Epsilon is the complement of the gamma [Bool] list, and one filterBits serves both ratings via the bit selector. Each column has one entry per row, and the list popCount calls testBit (via !!?) for each index, so each count is quadratic in row count and is recomputed several times per call. filterBits re-transposes every step, and loops forever if two or more identical rows remain.

2021/4.approach: Each board maps number to (x,y) in an IntMap plus a Set of marked cells; calls are folded over all boards, checking ten row/column lines for a win, dropping winners for part 2.
2021/4.critique: The number-to-position IntMap makes marking a single lookup, and the rows-plus-transpose trick builds the win lines compactly. isWon recomputes all 10 lines after every call instead of tracking line counts, and the 5x5 size is hard-coded. Parsing relies on exact spacing and parseWith calls error on failure; the Maybe result type only covers the no-winner case.

2021/5.approach: Parses each line into two endpoints sorted lexicographically, expands each segment into points with linePoints, keeps points appearing more than once via a Map-based duplicates helper, and counts them.
2021/5.critique: Lexicographic sorting makes x ascend, so axis lines use plain ranges; diagonals may still have descending y, which linePoints handles via signum (y2 - y1). The part1 filter built from split, &&&, both and same is harder to read than x1 == x2 || y1 == y2. duplicates costs O(P log P); toTuple2 errors unless exactly two coordinates, and parseWith calls error on parse failure.

2021/6.approach: Computes, per starting fish, the number of descendants after d days via a recursive count over (days remaining, timer), memoised with monad-memo, and sums over all fish in one shared memo table.
2021/6.critique: The recurrence is compact: a timer of 0 splits into (6, 8), and the single startEvalMemo means repeated timers reuse cached work, so the state space is at most d×9 entries. Each recursive step also goes through memo, adding Map overhead for chains a direct per-timer count vector or closed form would avoid. Timer constants 6 and 8 are hard-coded, and parsing errors call error.

2021/7.approach: Parses crab positions with a Parsec CSV parser, then sums fuel at the three positions within 1 of a centre (median for part 1, floored integer mean for part 2) and takes the minimum.
2021/7.critique: `solve` takes the centre and cost functions as arguments, so both parts share one routine: it computes the centre, then sums over the list once per candidate. Part 1 sorts first via `median`, so it costs O(n log n). Correctness depends on the optimum lying in the ±1 window, which the code neither states nor checks. `median` indexes with `!!` and `mean` divides by zero on empty input.

2021/8.approach: Each line is decoded by brute force: all 5040 permutations of the seven-segment enum are tried, and the first that maps every signal pattern onto a known digit set wins. It then decodes the four output digits.
2021/8.critique: Decoding happens inside the Parsec parser via `(p : _) <-`, so the parser itself solves the wiring; a compact design, but no matching permutation gives an opaque pattern-match failure. Brute force costs up to 5040×10 set maps per line, fine at this size. Part 1 runs the full part-2 decode just to count 1/4/7/8, where a segment-length check would do.

2021/9.approach: Parses the heightmap into a Map grid of DigitCell. Part 1 sums risk over cells lower than all orthogonal neighbours; part 2 runs a Seq-queue BFS from each minimum, stopping at cells equal to maxBound.
2021/9.critique: The basin wall is `maxBound` of the cell type, which for `DigitCell` comes from its derived `Bounded` instance rather than a literal 9. In `M.lookup n g >= M.lookup p g`, `p` is always on the grid, so an off-grid `n` gives `Nothing >= Just _`, which is False and drops it; this reliance on Maybe ordering is uncommented. The `&&& ... app` pipeline in part 1 is dense, and the input is parsed twice.

2021/10.approach: Each line runs through a stack-based bracket matcher that pushes expected closers and returns Left on the first mismatched character or Right with the leftover stack. Corrupt lines are scored by character and incomplete lines by base-5 folding plus a median.
2021/10.critique: Pushing the expected closer instead of the opener makes the leftover stack the completion string directly, so partitionEithers splits both parts in one pass. The single score table avoids two lookups. scoreLine's Applicative-Maybe fold is harder to read than a plain fold, and median relies on an odd-length list via partial (!!).

2021/11.approach: Simulates each step on a Map-based grid of Fin-10 digits. Incrementing wraps 9 to 0, so a cell at 0 has flashed. Flashes cascade by repeatedly bumping the neighbours of newly found zero cells until none remain.
2021/11.critique: Using `Fin Nat10` arithmetic removes the separate reset pass: wrapped cells are the flashes, and `flashIncrement` leaves zeros untouched. `M.adjust` silently ignores off-grid neighbours. Each cascade round rescans the whole map with `flippedLookupM`. Part 2 hard-codes 100 as the grid size and uses partial `(!! 0)`, and the generic signature hides its reliance on wraparound `Num`.

2021/12.approach: Breadth-first enumeration of every path from Start over an adjacency Map, using a Data.Sequence queue whose entries carry the reversed path and a Map of visit counts for small caves.
2021/12.critique: Both parts share one search, differing only in a predicate over the count values, which keeps the rule change to one line. Every complete path is built and kept as a list only to be counted with length, so memory grows with the answer. A count-only DFS memoised on (node, visited set) would be cheaper. The line `catMaybes (sequence (M.lookup ...))` is an obscure way to get neighbours. Nodes that toNode rejects are dropped silently, so toTuple2 fails without a clear error.

2021/13.approach: The parser turns each fold line into a function that reflects points beyond the line via 2c - v, and Relude's scanl' applies them to the dot Set, keeping every intermediate set.
2021/13.critique: Each fold is one S.map over the dots, not a dense grid, and the scanl' list serves part 1 (index 1) and part 2 (last). many1 guarantees a fold, so NE.fromList is safe. parseWith calls error on parse failure, toTuple2 on wrong field counts, and number's unsafe read on digit-dash strings like 1-2. The parser one-liner is dense, and part 2 must be read by eye.

2021/14.approach: Tracks counts of adjacent character pairs in a Map, rewriting each pair (a,b) into (a,c) and (c,b) per step, then halves per-letter pair counts and adds back the template's end characters.
2021/14.critique: Pair counting makes each step's work proportional to the number of distinct pairs (rebuilt via fromListWith), not the polymer length, which is what makes 40 steps feasible. The halving trick with +1 for first and last characters is correct but unexplained. `rules M.! [a,b]` is partial, assuming every pair has a rule.

2021/15.approach: Dijkstra with lazy deletion over a min-priority queue keyed by risk accumulated before entering a cell. Part 2 tiles the grid virtually with extendGrid and wraps risks above 9 by subtracting 9.
2021/15.critique: Each popped cell adds its own risk via lookup pos, with the origin special-cased to cost 0, and pushes all in-bounds neighbours at that total. extendGrid computes tiled values on demand through divMod tile offsets, so the 5x map is never built. Weaknesses: best-known risks live in a Map with O(log n) lookups, duplicate queue entries are only discarded when popped, and Data.Set is imported but unused.

2021/16.approach: Expands the hex line to a String of '0'/'1' characters, parses it with Parsec into a recursive Packet AST (literal groups, two length-type operator forms), then folds the tree for version sum or evaluation.
2021/16.critique: The ADT plus Parsec keeps parsing and evaluation separate, and the length-type-0 case reuses the parser by slicing the bits and re-parsing them with `parseWith (many packet)`. Weaknesses: bits are a list of Chars, `bitsToInt` on `[Bool]` is quadratic via `testBit`/`!!?`, and failures go through `error` in `opFromInt`, `toTuple2`, `hexToBin` and the nested `parseWith`.

2021/17.approach: Brute-forces launch velocities with vx from floor(1/4 + sqrt(1 + 8*minX)/2) to maxX and vy from minY to |minY|, simulating each until it lands in the hard-coded target or overshoots.
2021/17.critique: The vx lower bound uses the triangular-number formula to skip probes that stall before minX. The vy upper limit of |minY| is assumed, not derived in code. The target is hard-coded instead of parsed. The `vx == 0 && y < minY` guard is redundant because the next guard returns Nothing for the same cases. `L.maximum` is partial, and the bound relies on floating-point sqrt.

2021/18.approach: Snailfish numbers are binary trees with ID-tagged leaves. Explode finds the first depth-4 pair and locates its neighbours by ID position in the flattened leaf list; split rewrites the first leaf of 10 or more; reduce repeats until stable.
2021/18.critique: Unique leaf IDs plus derived Foldable give in-order neighbour lookup without zippers, and the Semigroup instance makes part 1 a plain fold. Each reduction step makes several linear passes (toList, elemIndex, mapID) plus structural equality checks to detect change. Part 2 filters pairs with derived structural `/=`, halving goes through Double, and toTuple2 is partial.

2021/19.approach: Scanners merge into scanner 0's growing beacon Set. Each scanner tries axis-permutation and sign-flip transforms, accepting an offset when one beacon difference appears 12 times (`nSameIn`), repeated via `iterateFix`.
2021/19.critique: Counting difference vectors in a Map with early exit is a short matcher. Putting `id` in the powerset list duplicates sign patterns, so 90 composed functions yield 48 distinct transforms, half of them reflections. Each remaining scanner's orientations are rebuilt every pass, comparing against the full merged set. Leftover unmatched scanners would silently undercount part 1.

2021/20.approach: Keeps the image in a coordinate Map grown one cell per side per step; fromListBE builds 9-bit indices, off-grid cells using a default from cycle [Cell False, Cell True].
2021/20.critique: Passing the off-grid default per step keeps background handling to one line. That default always alternates and is never read from alg, so it is only right for inputs whose first and last alg entries make the background flip. Each step rescans all keys for minXY/maxXY, does nine O(log n) Map lookups per cell, and rebuilds the Map with M.fromList, where an array would avoid these costs.

2021/21.approach: A lens-based Game record is advanced by `roll`. Part 1 recurses over an infinite cycled 1..100 die list. Part 2 recursively counts wins across all 27 three-roll outcomes, memoised on Game with monad-memo.
2021/21.critique: Tallying wins as (Sum Int, Sum Int) pairs combined with mconcat keeps part 2 short. Recursion stops once a score reaches 21, so the memo table is bounded by positions, scores below 21 and turn. It still explores 27 roll triples rather than 7 sums weighted by frequency. Starting positions are hard-coded literals instead of parsed input.

2021/22.approach: Part 1 folds every instruction over all cells of the 101³ cube. Part 2 uses inclusion–exclusion: each step appends the new cuboid if on, plus negated intersections with every stored cuboid, then sums signed volumes.
2021/22.critique: Half-open ranges from `(+ 1) <$> number` keep `volume` simple, and the signed-cuboid fold is short and correct. Each step walks all of `seen` and may add an entry per element, so the list can grow geometrically. With half-open ranges, `x0 <= x1` admits empty intersections; they add zero volume but still lengthen the list. Part 1 rewalks a million-element list per instruction.

2021/23.approach: A* over states mapping each amphipod type to a HashSet of coordinates, using a min-priority queue keyed on cost plus a per-amphipod distance-to-home-column estimate; a BFS per amphipod finds legal destinations.
2021/23.critique: Move legality sits in `getValidDestinations` (rooms only when holding no strangers, a fixed set of hallway stops) and `isFixed`, which keeps settled amphipods in place. Both mazes are hard-coded with walls padding part 1 to four rows so one `destinationMap` serves both parts. A `traceShow` prints on every expansion, and partial `HM.!`, `L.head` and `foldl1` appear throughout.

2021/24.approach: Parses the three per-digit constants from fixed line offsets of each 18-line block, then runs a digit-by-digit search over a Map from z value to digit list, keeping the max or min list per z.
2021/24.critique: Collapsing states by z with fromListWith max/min is a sound dynamic program and avoids interpreting the ALU generically. However, z is never bounded or pruned, so the frontier can grow very large. Parsing depends on hard-coded line indices 4, 5 and 15 and the 18-line block shape. Using `length ws` per entry and `intToDigit` round-tripping through Text are awkward.

2021/25.approach: Simulates the herd on a Map-based grid, moving east then south each step, then counts the leading pairs of consecutive grids in the lazy `iterate` sequence that differ.
2021/25.critique: Each half-step builds its move list from the pre-step grid, so simultaneous movement falls out naturally, and the answer comes from `takeWhile (uncurry (/=))` over adjacent grids, plus one. Every step rebuilds a persistent Map with O(n log n) inserts and compares whole maps. `g M.! n` is partial, though safe after `wrap`, and the `Bimap` and `foldl1'` imports are unused.

2022/1.approach: A Parsec parser reads blank-line-separated groups of numbers and sums each group with a double fmap; part 1 takes the maximum, and part 2 sorts descending and sums the top three.
2022/1.critique: The parser does both the grouping and the summing in one line, so each part is a short `&` pipeline over input embedded at compile time with Template Haskell. Part 2 sorts the whole list to get three values, which costs O(n log n) where a single pass would be O(n). `maximum` and `parseWith` are partial and call `error` on empty or malformed input.

2022/2.approach: Parses each line into two RPS values with Parsec, scores games using cyclic successor/predecessor on a Bounded Enum, and for part 2 rewrites the second move from the desired outcome before scoring.
2022/2.critique: Encoding the beats relation as succCyc on a three-constructor enum avoids a 9-case table, and both parts share one solve function. Part 2 reuses the RPS type to mean lose/draw/win, so updateEntry's Rock/Paper/Scissors patterns are misleading. The parser treats A and X interchangeably, and parseWith calls error on bad input.

2022/3.approach: Each line is cut in half with chunksOf, the halves become Data.Set values and are intersected; part 2 groups lines in threes, folds S.intersection over them, and scores letters by ord offsets.
2022/3.critique: Both parts are short point-free pipelines with the same set-intersection-then-head shape, though duplicate1 and duplicate2 are separate functions. U.head and toTuple2 are partial: an odd-length line such as length 5 gives chunks of 2, 2 and 1, so toTuple2 errors. priority relies on the bare offsets 96 and 38, and the unused chunk import is noise.

2022/4.approach: Parses each line with Parsec into a pair of integer intervals, then counts pairs where one interval contains the other (part 1) or where they intersect (part 2), using direct endpoint comparisons.
2022/4.critique: Both predicates are O(1) endpoint checks with no range expansion. The overlap test, which checks whether either start lies inside the other interval, is correct but less obvious than `c <= b && a <= d`. `sepBy` accepts any field count, so a line with the wrong number of fields reaches the partial `toTuple2` inside the parser and crashes. Syntax errors crash too, via `parseWith`'s `error`.

2022/5.approach: A Parsec parser reads eight crate rows, transposes them into a Vector of stacks, then folds the moves with V.//, taking the moved block as is or reversed.
2022/5.critique: Passing reverse or id as the only difference between parts keeps both answers in one solve function, and the generic numberLine3 makes move parsing short. The row count 8 is hard-coded, so the parser depends on input height. U.head crashes if a stack ends empty, and each V.// copies the whole vector, which is cheap only because there are few stacks.

2022/6.approach: Unpacks the embedded input to a String and recursively slides a window of n characters, returning the index past the first window whose nub length equals n, starting the counter at n.
2022/6.critique: Short and direct: starting the counter at n gives the answer position without extra arithmetic, and the trailing pattern returns Nothing instead of crashing. Each step runs quadratic nub on the window and calls length on take, so it costs O(len·n²), fine at n=14 but not incremental. The inner `as` shadows the outer argument, and Maybe Integer next to Int counts adds needless conversions.

2022/7.approach: Parses the terminal log with Parsec into Cd/Ls commands, replays them with a reversed path stack to build a rose tree of Dir/File nodes, then recomputes every directory's size recursively.
2022/7.critique: The tree type and parser are clear, and both parts reduce to a filter and fold over dirSizes. insertNode is partial (U.head crashes on an unseen directory) and uses structural delete, and dirSizes calls nodeSize per directory, giving quadratic work. mkFs drops the first command unchecked and treats any later `cd /` as a child name; 100000 and 40000000 are bare literals.

2022/8.approach: Part 1 folds each row and column in both directions, keeping coordinates that beat a running maximum. Part 2 sweeps each line tracking distance to the last tree of each height 0-9 and multiplies the four directional scores per cell.
2022/8.critique: Part 2's per-height table makes each sweep O(10) per cell instead of rescanning, so the whole thing is linear in grid size times 10. However, `nub` over the visible-coordinate list is quadratic where a Set would do. `visibilityFrom` has no empty-list case, and `U.head`/`U.last` are partial. Cell 9 is hard-coded as the maximum height. The `fst3`/`<$$>` fold state is dense to read.

2022/9.approach: `foldl'` over parsed moves calls `moveRope`, which recurses once per unit step: it shifts the head, lets each knot follow by clipping the per-axis delta to [-1,1], and prepends the new tail position.
2022/9.critique: Clipping each axis delta with `clip` expresses the follow rule in one expression, and `solve n` handles both parts. The answer comes from `nub` on the full path, which is O(n²); a `Set` would make it O(n log n). Also, `moveTail` takes a `d` parameter it never uses, adjacency is checked with `elem` over `a : neighbors a` rather than a Chebyshev-distance comparison, and the fold carries an anonymous tuple.

2022/10.approach: A strict left fold over parsed instructions records the X register value during every cycle in a Map; part 1 sums signal strengths at fixed cycles, and part 2 renders lit pixels via the Grid helper.
2022/10.critique: Logging X once per cycle (twice for addx) produces one trace that serves both parts. The Map is unnecessary because cycles are inserted in order, so a list would do. The checkpoints [20,60,...,220] and the screen width 40 are literals. fromCoords sizes the grid to the largest lit coordinate, so trailing dark columns or rows are dropped, and parseWith calls error on bad input.

2022/11.approach: Parses each monkey into a positional `Monkey` constructor holding an item Seq, operation and target-choice closures, and a throw counter, then simulates rounds over a Map using `iterate`.
2022/11.critique: Building the operation and test as closures during parsing keeps the simulation short. Reducing worry modulo the product of all divisors keeps part 2 numbers small. The constructor fields are lazy, so the `n + 1` counters may build thunk chains, and `iterate ... !! 10000` defers evaluation. Monkey ids are assumed to run 0..n-1, and `M.!` is partial.

2022/12.approach: Breadth-first search backwards from the End cell over a Map-based grid with a reversed climb rule, stopping at the first cell matching a predicate: Start for part 1, a plain 'a' cell for part 2.
2022/12.critique: One `floodUntil` serves both parts, and S and E carry heights 'a' and 'z' in their `_c` fields. Out-of-grid neighbours are dropped because the step test compares `Maybe` values, where `Nothing < Just _`, which is a subtle way to bounds-check. Part 2's `(== Cell 'a')` excludes `Start 'a'` as a target. Visited checks happen on dequeue, so duplicates enter the Seq, and the grid is parsed twice.

2022/13.approach: A recursive Parsec parser builds a Packet tree; a hand-written cmp gives the ordering, part 1 sums indices of LT pairs, part 2 sorts all packets plus dividers and multiplies divider positions.
2022/13.critique: The cmp function maps the comparison rules directly onto pattern matches, promoting a lone integer to a one-element list, and the pipelines read clearly. Part 2 sorts everything in O(n log n) when counting packets below each divider would be linear. Parsing relies on partial toTuple2 and an error-throwing parseWith, and cmp could have been an Ord instance.

2022/14.approach: Parses rock paths into coordinate lists, passes them to Helper.Grid.fromCoords (which fills the bounding box from (0,0) with Empty), then drops grains via iterate over Maybe Grid until one escapes or the source fills.
2022/14.critique: One solve serves both parts by appending a floor row, and Maybe gives a clean stop signal. Each grain is re-simulated from (500,0) rather than resuming from the previous path. fromCoords stores every cell from x=0 to maxX, not just rocks. Part 2 hard-codes floor width 0..1000, and dropGrain treats missing cells as blocked.

2022/15.approach: Part 1 builds a Set of every covered x on row 2000000 per sensor, unions them and counts. Part 2 runs best-first search from the grid centre, prioritising cells by how many sensors cover them.
2022/15.critique: Part 1 materialises millions of points in Sets instead of merging intervals, so it is memory-heavy. Part 2's priority-queue search on coverage count has no guarantee of reaching a zero-score cell quickly, and each pushed cell rescans all sensors. Constants 2000000/4000000 are hard-coded, foldl1 fails on an empty list, and parse errors abort via error.

2022/16.approach: Part 1 runs a breadth-first search over (valve, open set, flow, total, time) states, pruned by the best total per (valve, open set). Part 2 enumerates single-agent opening schedules over BFS distances and pairs the top 250.
2022/16.critique: Part 1's cache stores only the total per (valve, open set), not time, so pruning relies on BFS order. singlePaths can insert openings later than the limit, which score weights negatively by `limit - t`. Part 2 keeps a hard-coded `take 250` with no stated guarantee of optimality. shortestPaths uses per-path seen sets, so it expands redundant paths.

2022/17.approach: Simulates falling rocks in a Map-based grid with lazily cycled jets and pieces. Part 2 stops when an undercounted move tally hits a jet-length multiple as the piece cycle restarts, then multiplies that height and adds a fresh remainder simulation.
2022/17.critique: Collision and push checks are direct and readable. Part 1 drops a hard-coded 485 pieces instead of 2022. Part 2's counter skips each rock's final jet, and assuming the tower repeats from an empty floor, with no profile check, is unsound, as the wrong-answer comments show. maxXY rescans all keys per rock; drop is copied three times.

2022/18.approach: Part 1 sums six minus occupied neighbours per cube via Set lookups. Part 2 starts a size-capped BFS flood fill from every cell of a hard-coded box, subtracting faces touching each bounded region found.
2022/18.critique: Part 1 is a straightforward O(n log n) count over a Data.Set. Part 2 is fitted to one input: the 1..18/0..19 box, the 3500-cell cap where interiorArea returns Nothing and the result is dropped, and the fixups (halving count key 10, inserting 1196) are unexplained constants. Every box coordinate, including lava cells, launches a flood, so regions are re-filled many times; fst3/snd3/thd3 are imported unused.

2022/19.approach: Best-first branch-and-bound over 9-tuple states in a max-priority queue keyed by an optimistic geode estimate; it stops once the best queued bound cannot beat the best geode count found.
2022/19.critique: The obsidian-limited upper bound and early exit prune strongly. The `seen` check compares only resources under the same robot counts, ignores `t`, and overwrites rather than merges entries. No `t == duration` cutoff exists, so stopping depends on the bound test. There is no max-spend robot cap, and the 9-tuples hurt readability.

2022/20.approach: Builds a circular doubly linked list in an immutable Vector of (value, prevIndex, nextIndex) triples, unlinks each element, walks |n| mod (len-1) links to the new spot, and relinks.
2022/20.critique: Indexing nodes by original position makes mixing order trivial, and reducing the step count mod (len-1) keeps part 2 walks bounded. But each V.// copies the whole vector, so a mix costs O(n²) in copies plus walking, where a mutable vector would avoid that. The irrefutable Just pattern for zeroI and list (!!) on a cycled list are partial and slow.

2022/21.approach: Parses each monkey into a closure over the monkey map and evaluates root by recursive lookup. Part 2 binary-searches humn over [0, 2^64] using root's comparison of its two operands.
2022/21.critique: Each closure looks up its own operands, so the Map is both the parse result and the evaluator, and swapping humn is a single M.insert. There is no memoisation, so every probe re-walks the tree. The search fixes one direction (LT narrows to the lower half) without checking it, assumes a non-negative answer below 2^64, and on EQ shrinks b by one instead of returning the matching m.

2022/22.approach: Parses the map into a padded Map-based grid and the path with Parsec, then walks step by step, delegating off-map moves to a wrapper: linear scan for part 1, hand-coded cube-edge table for part 2.
2022/22.critique: Parametrising followPath over a Wrapper keeps both parts on one walker. Part 2 is a fourteen-guard table for one 50-wide net, with start (50,0), 200 grid rows and edge offsets hard-coded. With no otherwise clause, a differently shaped net can reach an unmatched guard and crash. The last guard's x < 100 is redundant given x == 49, and linearWrap rescans a row or column on every wrap.

2022/23.approach: Simulates rounds as a lazy infinite list of Set Coord2 states; each elf proposes via the rotating direction order, countMap rejects collided targets, part 2 finds the first unchanged consecutive pair.
2022/23.critique: The lazy `steps` stream is shared by both parts, and the 'all four directions free means stay' rule is folded neatly into the `[_, _, _, _]` pattern. Weaknesses: part 1 materialises a filled bounding-box Map instead of computing area minus elf count, each round rebuilds an O(n log n) Map plus full Set equality, and `!!`, `M.!`, `U.head` are partial.

2022/24.approach: Precomputes one blizzard Map-grid per minute over a period of lcm (w - 1) (h - 1), then runs A* (min-priority queue, Manhattan heuristic) over (position, time mod period) states, chaining three searches for part 2.
2022/24.critique: Caching grids for the full period makes each lookup cheap and keeps the seen set finite, and part 2 reuses the search by rotating the cycled grid list by elapsed time. The cost is memory: one full Map per minute, rebuilt separately in each part. The `let Blizzard ds = v` binding is a partial pattern, guarded only by the preceding `isBlizzard` filter.

2022/25.approach: Decodes each SNAFU line by recursing over reversed digits, adding digit value times 5^n, then sums. Encoding finds the digit count from repeated '2' strings and picks digits greedily from the top.
2022/25.critique: Decoding is plain place-value recursion with an explicit accumulator in `go`. Encoding picks each digit by whether the remaining magnitude exceeds 2·(sum of lower powers), the most the lower digits can cover. The greedy step recomputes `sum ps` at every digit, making it quadratic in digit count, though counts are small. `snafuVal` is partial and `U.head` is unsafe.

2023/1.approach: Each line is scanned with replace-megaparsec's sepCap for digit (and, in part 2, spelled-number) matches; the first match comes from the forward line, the last from parsing the reversed line against reversed words.
2023/1.critique: Parsing the reversed line against reversed number words handles overlapping spellings like 'twone' without lookahead. Running sepCap over the whole line only to take the head does extra work, but it is linear and harmless here. uhead is partial, so a line with no match crashes. Input is embedded at compile time via Template Haskell.

2023/2.approach: A parser-combinator grammar builds Game records holding lists of Color draws. Part 1 keeps games whose draws stay within fixed limits; part 2 flattens draws and multiplies per-colour maxima.
2023/2.critique: The Color sum type and the explicit three-accumulator go loop for r/g/b keep both parts short, linear in input, and easy to follow. The 12/13/14 limits are hard-coded literals. Input is spliced at compile time via Template Haskell, and because (⊢) returns a plain value rather than an Either or Maybe, the caller cannot handle a parse failure.

2023/3.approach: Scans the grid row by row, accumulating each digit run's characters and neighbour coordinates, then nubs them; part 1 keeps numbers bordering any Mark, part 2 groups numbers by adjacent '*' cells.
2023/3.critique: The hand-written scanner repeats the same flush logic at a non-digit cell and at the row end. Neighbour lists grow by repeated list appends and are deduplicated with quadratic nub, while out-of-bounds coordinates are handled by catMaybes over (||?). Part 2 builds a per-number Map, merges with unionWith (<>), and keeps gears with exactly two numbers; foldl1 is partial if the grid has no numbers.

2023/4.approach: Parses each card into an id and two number lists split at `|`; part 1 sums `2 ^ size (as ∩ bs) `div` 2`, part 2 folds over cards, adding each card's count to the next n card ids in a Map.
2023/4.critique: The `2 ^ n `div` 2` form gives 0 for n = 0 without a branch, and one `parser` serves both parts. Part 2 uses an outer `foldl'` over cards and an inner `foldl'` over `[i + 1 .. i + n]` applying `adjust (+ c)`, so copies propagate forward as counts without materialising cards. Part 1 calls `parseWith parser` while part 2 uses the `⊢` operator for the same step, an inconsistency.

2023/5.approach: Each map line becomes a forward and inverse partial function, combined per section as first-match-or-identity. Part 1 folds seeds forward; part 2 takes each line's first number as a candidate and checks it against the seed ranges.
2023/5.critique: A single lambda over the swapped (source, dest) pairs produces both directions, so neither is written twice. Part 2 tests only the per-line dest numbers, combining the sections' inverse functions with `Ɍ ($)`. Range lookups scan linearly, the seed check rebuilds `chunksOf 2 seeds` for every candidate, and `toTuple2` is partial.

2023/6.approach: Parses times and distances as Doubles, solves the quadratic x(t−x) > d in closed form, and counts integers strictly between the roots via ceiling/floor; part 2 concatenates digits and reparses.
2023/6.critique: The quadratic formula makes each race O(1), so part 2 needs no search, and `ceiling − floor − 1` counts only integers strictly between the roots, so exact integer roots are excluded correctly. All arithmetic, including the square root, is done in Double rather than integers. `asOne` builds the part-2 race by going through `round`, `show` and `uread` on each column, which works but is indirect.

2023/7.approach: Cards and hand types are enums with derived Ord. A tuple compare of (hand type, cards) sorts hands. Part 2 wraps cards in a JCard newtype that ranks jokers lowest and maps each type and joker count to an upgraded type. The sorted list is zipped with ranks.
2023/7.critique: Using Ord instances and newtypes means the sort does all the ranking work. The joker upgrade is a hand-written case table over count patterns, which is long and easy to get wrong where a rule like 'add jokers to the largest group' would be shorter. charToCard and the Pair/TwoPair case are partial, and the parser also computes the final sum.

2023/8.approach: Parses the instruction string and node map with parser combinators, then lazily walks the cyclic L/R list to emit every step count at which a goal predicate holds. Part 2 takes each 'A'-ending start's first hit and folds them with lcm.
2023/8.critique: Having travel return a lazy infinite list of hit times keeps one walker for both parts, with uhead taking the first hit. Part 2 combines only each start's first hit via lcm and never inspects later hits from the same list. The non-exhaustive case on 'L'/'R' and the (!! 2) indexing are partial functions.

2023/9.approach: Each line is parsed into integers. A foldl' runs length−1 times, prepending successive difference rows, then foldr1 and the operator ((+) part 1, (-) part 2) combine each row's last or first element.
2023/9.critique: Both parts share one solve, parameterised only by the element selector and the combining operator. It always builds all length−1 difference rows, so each line costs quadratic time and it never stops early when a row turns all zero. The whole pipeline in solve is a single point-free line of &&&, uncurry and flip, which makes the operand order of the final combination hard to follow.

2023/10.approach: Walks the loop from S in both directions, marking one side of each pipe as candidate outside cells. It BFS flood-fills non-loop regions, discards any region touching a marked cell, then drops whichever result contains (0,0).
2023/10.critique: Marking a side of the loop during the walk replaces a separate shoelace or ray-casting pass, and the two walk directions cover both orientations. Choosing between the results by testing (0,0) assumes that cell is off the loop, so it sits in the exterior. The point-free part2 pipeline, built from both, &&& and uncurry, is hard to follow.

2023/11.approach: Builds two sets of empty line indices, one per coordinate axis, then for every unordered galaxy pair walks each axis's coordinate range, counting 1 per index or the scale factor for empty ones.
2023/11.critique: One function parameterised by the expansion factor serves both parts, and the inclusive `range` walk with a `- 2` correction handles endpoints uniformly. The empty-line sets are built inside the per-pair function `d`, so each pair rescans the grid unless GHC floats them out. The range walk is also linear in coordinate differences, where prefix sums over sorted coordinates would avoid that.

2023/12.approach: Memoised recursion keyed on (remaining string, remaining group sizes): a leading '.' is prepended, each group is placed after a gap of i non-'#' cells, and recursive counts are summed. Part two unfolds records fivefold.
2023/12.critique: Prepending '.' makes every placement a uniform gap-then-block step, keeping the recursion to two clauses. The memo key holds the whole string suffix, so key comparisons cost more as strings grow. For each candidate i it builds a Set from the gap take i ss and another from the block take c (drop i ss), and it tries every i rather than stopping once the gap hits a '#'.

2023/13.approach: Each candidate vertical and horizontal mirror line is checked by comparing the cell blocks on either side. Part 2 toggles every cell, recomputes reflections, and keeps lines absent from the original grid.
2023/13.critique: Both axes are handled in one comprehension tagged Left/Right, so no code is duplicated, and partitionEithers keeps the final sum short. Part 2 is brute force, rerunning the full reflection scan once per toggled cell instead of finding lines with exactly one mismatch. The dense operators and the index arithmetic in `b` make the mirrored ranges hard to verify.

2023/14.approach: Tilts by repeating a single-cell roll pass (`step`) over a VectorGrid until it stops changing (`iterateFix`), then sums row-weighted loads; part 2 indexes the `iterate oneCycle` sequence at 1000000000 using `(...)`.
2023/14.critique: One `step` serves all four directions via `move`, `opposite` and `iterCoords`, keeping both parts short. Each tilt runs whole-grid passes until a fixpoint and compares full grids with `Eq` after every pass, rather than sliding rocks in one sweep. Part 2 relies on `(...)` selecting the 1000000000th element; its `Ord` constraint suggests repeat detection, but the shortcut is not visible here.

2023/15.approach: Part 1 sums the HASH of each comma-separated step. Part 2 parses steps and folds them into 256 boxes, each a Map from label to focal length plus a Seq for lens order.
2023/15.critique: Keeping a label-to-focal Map beside a Seq of labels separates lookup from ordering: '=' on an existing label rewrites only the Map entry, so the Seq order is preserved without searching it. Encoding '-' as ('-', 0) via pure 0 keeps one tuple type. The bool-based branches, with argument order (false, true), are harder to read than guards.

2023/16.approach: Worklist traversal over (coordinate, direction) states, destructured with `Empty`/`:<|` and extended with `<⊕`, recording a visited set and mapping each tile character to outgoing directions; part 2 maximises over perimeter starts.
2023/16.critique: The mirror and splitter rules fit in one case expression, with `bool` choosing the turn per incoming axis, and keying `seen` on (cell, direction) stops beams from looping forever. Part 2 runs `energized` from scratch for each direction paired with the perimeter cells `pFrom` gives for it, a straightforward brute force. The case has no fallback branch, so an unexpected character crashes at runtime.

2023/17.approach: A* search over states (cell, current run length, direction) using a min-priority queue and Manhattan-distance heuristic, with turn and continue rules passed in as predicates for each part.
2023/17.critique: One search serves both parts through the turnP/noTurnP predicates, and the goal check reuses turnP to enforce part 2's minimum run. Cost is charged on the cell being left and corrected at the goal by adding the target and subtracting the origin, which works but is hard to follow. Duplicate states are pruned only when popped, so the queue grows, and `(q <!)` is partial if no path exists.

2023/18.approach: Parses each line into two (direction, length) instructions, selects one per part, then walks the polygon accumulating a shoelace-style area term and perimeter, combining them via Pick's theorem.
2023/18.critique: One parser and one fold serve both parts, and accumulating `x' * (y' - y)` plus `p div 2 + 1` handles the large part 2 coordinates in O(n) without a grid. The area term is used without `abs`, so the sign depends on traversal orientation, which the code does not check. The part 2 direction comes from indexing the hard-coded list `[DirRight, DirDown, DirLeft, DirUp]` with a parsed `number`, a partial `!!` lookup.

2023/19.approach: Each rule is parsed once into a pair of a predicate closure and a symbolic condition; part 1 runs parts through the closures, part 2 walks backward from "A" over rule-prefix paths, intersecting xmas ranges.
2023/19.critique: Building both representations in one parser pass serves both parts, and the backward search uses a map of paths keyed by destination; negating earlier conditions with `invert` gives disjoint ranges without forward interval splitting. Part 1's `uhead` fails if no rule in a workflow matches, and `|!` lookups assume every target exists. The 1–4000 bounds and "in" start are hard-coded.

2023/20.approach: Simulates pulses with a FIFO Seq queue per button press, timestamping each module's outputs; for each predecessor of hard-coded 'vf', takes the first output change's later press index plus 1, then multiplies.
2023/20.critique: The per-module (press, signal) history makes part 2 a scan for the first output flip. Each processed pulse conses a full state map onto `ss`, never trimmed, and `stateChanges` reruns the 5000-press simulation once per predecessor. The 'vf' name and 5000 bound are input-specific, and `let Just (ts, fullName)` and `uhead` are partial.

2023/21.approach: Both parts expand a Set of reachable plots one step at a time. Part 2 tiles the grid via modular lookups, records set sizes when `n mod 131 == 65` (steps 65, 196, 327), and extrapolates quadratically.
2023/21.critique: The frontier-set simulation is short, and a finite-difference quadratic fit avoids simulating 26501365 steps. The constants 131, 65 and 393 are hard-coded, and the extrapolation assumes the counts grow quadratically at those intervals, which the code does not check. Each step rebuilds a Set from all neighbours, `let [a, b, c]` is a partial pattern, and `do` wraps a pure value.

2023/22.approach: Bricks are sorted by z and settled by repeated passes that lower each unsupported brick one unit until a fixpoint. Pairwise support maps answer part 1 and drive an iterated fallen-set expansion for part 2.
2023/22.critique: Two Map Brick (Set Brick) support relations make both parts short comprehensions, and endpoint order is normalised with min/max. Settling is slow: a pass moves each brick at most one unit with an O(n) any-check per brick. The maps need O(n²) pairwise tests, and part 2 re-filters the surviving set every round for each starting brick.

2023/23.approach: Part 1 enumerates paths with a queue of (cell, visited-set) states, moving any direction on '.' but only arrow-wise on slopes. Part 2 builds a junction graph (convolution-found forks plus start/end) and runs exhaustive DFS.
2023/23.critique: Junction compression keeps Part 2's exhaustive search tractable. mkGraph runs a full slopePaths search for every junction pair from triPairs, adjacent or not, repeating grid work. Part 1 keeps every complete path set in memory before taking the maximum length. maximum and |! are partial, and -1 stands in for no path.

2023/24.approach: Part 1 intersects every hailstone pair's 2D slope-intercept lines over exact rationals, filtering by bounds and future time; part 2 gives Z3 position-plus-velocity equations for all stones.
2023/24.critique: Exact rationals avoid floating-point error, and Z3 solves part 2 with little algebra. `t'` is computed from the first stone's `x` and `vx`, duplicating `t`; the second stone's future check really comes from its own `validIntersection` call, where `inFuture` uses its values. A zero x- or y-velocity can divide by zero. Part 2 adds a time variable per stone where three stones suffice.

2023/25.approach: Parses lines into (node, neighbours) pairs, builds an adjacency map with mkMap and a reversed one with swapMapList, merges them via unionWith (<>), then counts nodes reachable while skipping three literal edges.
2023/25.critique: The three cut edges are hard-coded node-name literals, so nothing computes the minimum cut and the solution depends on a specific input's edge names. The traversal is short: a queue matched with Empty and :<| plus a visited set, multiplying component size by the remainder. `count 3 alphaNum` assumes three-character names.

2024/1.approach: Parses the input into number pairs and unzips them into two lists. Part 1 sorts both and sums `diff` over the zipped pairs. Part 2 counts the right list and sums each left value times its count.
2024/1.critique: Each part fits on one line, and `twoOf` with `unzip` keeps parsing compact. Sorting costs O(n log n), and the count map avoids a quadratic scan. Part 2 is hard to read: `counts <$> lists` counts only the right list via the tuple Functor, then `&<@>`, `<.>`, a flipped `|?` and `? 0` follow, and decoding it needs the prelude's signatures.

2024/2.approach: A recursive parser reads numbers one at a time, prepending each to the accumulated list. With `skip` set, an alternative consumes one `anyWord` and continues with skipping disabled.
2024/2.critique: The guard multiplies every difference by each distinct sign and requires all products to lie in [1,2,3], so mixed signs or a zero difference fail and one check enforces both direction and step size. Tolerance is just another `trying` alternative. `diffs` is recomputed over the whole accumulated list at each step rather than incrementally.

2024/3.approach: A recursive parser tries ordered alternatives at each position: do() and don't() set an enabled flag, mul(a,b) yields a Σ of Π values, any other character is skipped, and |-<.> runs the parser on the input.
2024/3.critique: One parser serves both parts. The first Bool is the state don't() switches to, so part 1 passes True and effectively ignores don't. A disabled mul still parses but produces Σ [Π 0] instead of being dropped, and the Σ/Π wrappers express the sum-of-products. The paired Bool parameters are cryptic, and the anyChar fallback means the parser advances one character at a time through junk input.

2024/4.approach: Each Text argument is parsed with readGrid; every grid from its rotations list goes to convolveWith as the first argument, with the $(grid 4) splice second; result cells are folded into a Σ ℤ total via its Monoid instance.
2024/4.critique: One function serves both parts: part 1 passes two text grids (a straight one and a diagonal one with '_' cells), part 2 one. Because rotations returns a list of same-typed grids, the applicative <$>/<*> yields one convolution per rotation and avoids per-direction code. The type-level arity (@n via variadicat) and the compile-time splice add machinery that makes the call sites harder to read.

2024/5.approach: Parses the `|` lines into a Map from each left-hand page to its right-hand pages, sorts each update with a comparator built from that map, and sums middle elements of unchanged (part 1) or reordered (part 2) updates.
2024/5.critique: Sorting with the rule-derived comparator and comparing against the original lets one `solve` helper handle both parts. `mkCompare` only checks whether `b` is listed under `a`, so a pair with no rule either way gets GT in both orders, which is not a lawful ordering; the results rely on every pair in an update having a rule. Membership is a linear list scan. The local `solve` shadows quaalude's Z3 `solve`.

2024/6.approach: Simulates the guard with a Set of (position, direction) states, returning Nothing on a repeat. Part 2 reruns the walk with '#' at each visited position, counting Nothing results minus one.
2024/6.critique: A single `walk` serves both parts, since a repeated (cell, direction) state means a loop. Part 2 reruns the whole simulation once per visited position. The fold starts at (-1) with no comment explaining the offset. The point-free `walk'`, built from `>>>` and `(+)`, is hard to read.

2024/7.approach: Each line's numbers go through `snoc`; `f` recurses over the list with `0` as its other argument, expanding every operator via `(ops >>=)`, and `Σ t` is summed when `t` is a result.
2024/7.critique: Passing the operator list into `with` lets both parts share one evaluator, with operator choices expanded by list-monad bind. It is brute force: all operator combinations are generated and membership of `t` is tested only at the end. Part 2's `||` builds `show a <> show b` and parses that string with `number`. The point-free composition in `f` is dense to read.

2024/8.approach: Converts the grid with `co` into a `Map Char` of positions, drops '.', forms all ordered position pairs per character via `join cartesian`, generates `b + (i,i)⋅(b-a)` over a range of i, deduplicates, and counts in-grid points.
2024/8.critique: Both parts share `step`. Part 1 passes the fixed range [1..1]. Part 2 uses `$$@` to apply one grid value twice, once to derive a single global bound from `maxXY` and once as input. That bound exceeds what pairs with larger offsets need, so their extra points are discarded by the membership test. List `nub` is quadratic where a set would not be, and the point-free chain is hard to follow without quaalude's definitions.

2024/9.approach: After prepending '0', the input parses as (gap, file) length pairs. Gaps go into a min-priority queue keyed by start, and each file range is placed in the leftmost gap before it that fits.
2024/9.critique: One function solves both parts. Files are fed last-first; part 1 splits each into single-block ranges, part 2 keeps whole ranges. Each range's checksum comes in closed form from triangular numbers. In place, too-small gaps before a file are popped and reinserted on the way back, so in part 2 one move can cost time linear in the earlier gaps. The point-free tuple pipeline (bimap, &@, $@, <:>, swap) is dense.

2024/10.approach: From each height-0 cell, a queue search over a Seq follows 4-neighbours exactly one higher and collects reached 9s in a list. Part 1 nubs it; part 2 counts it.
2024/10.critique: A skip flag and post-processing function let one traversal serve both parts. Part 2 never checks seen, so cells are re-expanded each time they are popped and work grows with trail count rather than grid size. Part 1 always passes skip=True, and the seen check runs before the 9 guard, so nines has no duplicates there and nub is redundant. The point-free chaining in hike is hard to read.

2024/11.approach: Each parsed stone becomes an `Mℤ n S` key (blinks left, plus `S`, a `Dℤ`-wrapped digit sequence built by `mkS`). A memoised `blink` is traversed over all stones, and the joined result sequence's `size` is returned.
2024/11.critique: Keeping digits as a sequence makes the even-length split a plain `halve` and the length test a `size` call. Memoising on (blinks left, stone) lets 75 blinks finish. But `blink` returns `Seq S`, concatenated with `(><)`, so memo entries hold stone sequences rather than counts. Results are counted only at the end with `size`. The `Mℤ`/`Dℤ` wrappers and `Dec` arithmetic obscure the rules.

2024/12.approach: Repeatedly picks an unvisited cell and flood-fills its region with a Seq queue, accumulating area, perimeter and outward boundary segments, then counts sides by grouping segments by direction and splitting them into contiguous runs.
2024/12.critique: One flood fill collects area, perimeter and boundary data. Keying segments by outward normal through `mkWith` keeps opposite edges of a thin strip apart, so a later sort and group finds straight runs. A cell can be enqueued several times before the membership guard skips it. The view-pattern guard and `<$@>` / `<>!` operators make the sides step hard to follow.

2024/13.approach: Runs gradient descent per machine on squared distance to the prize plus 3a+b, stepping by 0.001 times the gradient divided by ax and bx; stops on an exact hit or when the loss is unchanged from the previous step.
2024/13.critique: Gradient descent is an unusual choice for a 2×2 linear system that Cramer's rule would solve exactly in constant time. Stopping when the loss equals the previous loss, or when the presses converted to integers hit the prize exactly, can miss solutions because of float error. The lens traversal adding 10^13 to indices 4 and 5 is compact. Any short final chunk from chunksOf 6 would crash the partial six-element match.

2024/14.approach: Simulates robots with modular wraparound, counts quadrants after 100 steps, then iterates until successive symmetric KL divergences of the robots' x+y histogram against the grid's differ by at least 0.6.
2024/14.critique: Part 2 projects robots onto anti-diagonals and measures symmetric KL divergence against the trapezoidal x+y distribution of all grid cells, so a large change between consecutive steps flags the clustered picture without image heuristics. The 0.6 threshold and the 101x103 dimensions are hard-coded constants. Using a list as a four-counter accumulator is less clear than a tuple, and logBase (exp 1) is a roundabout natural log.

2024/15.approach: Simulates the robot on a grid, recursively collecting the layer of box cells each push reaches until hitting walls or empty space, then applying the resulting list of grid-update functions to the grid.
2024/15.critique: One `step` handles both parts: `affected` adds the partner half only for vertical pushes of `[`/`]`, and `nub` stops a shared box being pushed twice. Each layer's move is a partially applied `movs` (`flip $ foldl' ...`) waiting for the grid; `foldl' (&) g moves` applies them farthest layer first, a compact but indirect encoding. `wide` omits `OL`/`OR`, safe only because they never appear before widening.

2024/16.approach: Compresses the maze into a graph of junctions joined by straight corridors that store their tile sets, then runs a priority-queue search ordered by cost plus a turn-and-distance estimate over (position, facing) states carrying accumulated tiles.
2024/16.critique: Storing corridor tiles on edges keeps the graph small, and the finished routes' tile sets are unioned once at the end, so no backtracking pass is needed. The seen map keeps the first cost popped per state and drops other costs, so part 2 relies on the estimate in `h` never popping a state above its optimal cost. Each queued state copies a Set, and `foldl1` is partial if no route exists.

2024/17.approach: f₁ is a hard-coded formula giving one output digit from register A. Part 1's f shifts A right three bits per digit; part 2's allA rebuilds A three bits at a time from the last digit backwards.
2024/17.critique: allA extends each candidate by eight 3-bit suffixes, keeps those whose f₁ output matches the next digit, explores every surviving branch through list-monad bind and takes the minimum. f₁ hard-codes one specific program (xor constants 3 and 5), and the parsed program serves only as part 2's target without ever being interpreted. The precedence-dependent one-liner in f₁ is hard to read.

2024/18.approach: scanl' builds one grid per prefix of falling bytes. A* ordered by steps plus Manhattan distance returns the reversed path to the goal, whose size answers part 1. Part 2 searches for the first unreachable index.
2024/18.critique: Precomputing all prefix grids lets `paths n` fetch grid `n + 1` directly, but each searchFromTo probe still runs a full A*. `path` accepts a step-indexed vector of grids, yet callers wrap one grid in `pure`, so the `min` clamp is dead generality. The `n + 1` and `? -1` offsets are hard to verify, and 70 and 1024 are hard-coded.

2024/19.approach: A memoised recursion counts the ways each design can be built by stripping towel prefixes. Each count n becomes the pair (signum n, n), and the pairs are monoid-summed to give both parts.
2024/19.critique: The (signum, count) pair under the Σ monoid answers both parts in one pass. The .=<<. memo combinator keeps the recursion close to the recurrence, with the empty design as base case. Nearly every token is a custom operator or point-free composition, so the data flow is hard to follow without quaalude.

2024/20.approach: Walks the corridor from S to E by repeatedly taking the single unvisited open neighbour, indexes each path cell by its distance from E, then pairs each cell with every cell nearer E within the cheat's Manhattan radius.
2024/20.critique: The `let [n] = ...` pattern assumes exactly one open unvisited neighbour at each step and crashes otherwise. The pair scan is O(N²) over path cells, with no spatial pruning. `size path - cost` is the true saving plus one, so the test also accepts savings of `threshold - 1`; the code alone does not rule out such cases.

2024/21.approach: A queue-driven search records every neighbour walk between keys up to a length cap, then keeps all tied shortest walks per key pair. A memoised recursion picks the cheapest candidate, costing each move at the next layer.
2024/21.critique: Memoising the inner `go'` on (layer, path) through `.$.` makes 25 layers cheap. Keeping every tied shortest path avoids hard-coding a move order. The search does not stop at the first shortest walks. It collects every gap-avoiding walk under the rows+cols−1 cap, including back-and-forth ones, then sorts, wasting work on tiny pads. Type-level keypad alphabets add machinery.

2024/22.approach: Part 1 iterates the shift/xor/prune step with scanl'. Part 2 maps each four-change window to its price per buyer via mkMap over the reversed window list, then tries every distinct window across all buyers.
2024/22.critique: Reversing before mkMap appears meant to make the earliest occurrence win, assuming mkMap keeps the last duplicate as Data.Map.fromList does. Part 2 is slow: an Eq-only nub over every buyer's keys is quadratic in the number of windows, and each candidate is then looked up in every buyer's map. Merging the per-buyer maps with a summing union would avoid both.

2024/23.approach: Builds a symmetric adjacency map, then grows cliques level by level, extending each by every vertex adjacent to all members; part 1 filters 3-cliques, part 2 takes the last level.
2024/23.critique: Each level is a Set of Sets, so permutations collapse and the scanl' yields each clique once, with both parts reusing one list. Growth is brute force: every clique is tested against every vertex each round. The `where` binding `(cl : cls)` is a refutable list pattern that would fail at runtime on an empty graph, and `clique !! 2` relies on index 2 being the 3-clique level.

2024/24.approach: Part 1 recursively evaluates every z wire over the gate map. Part 2 builds expression trees for all circuit keys, diffs them against a generated ripple-carry adder, and records swaps recursively until the adder matches or eight entries exist.
2024/24.critique: Comparing trees with commutative matching (diffTree) against a reference adder finds swaps structurally, not by brute force. Wire evaluation is unmemoised, and each fixAdd call re-parses the input. The nested let pattern is refutable and fails if getclosest returns nothing. swaptext and treeIn (which has a duplicated clause) are never called by part1 or part2, the local !+! is unused, and traceShow calls remain in part2's path.

2024/25.approach: Parses all schematics into typed grids, forms pairs with triPairs, and counts a pair when the cell pair ('#','#') is absent from the zip of the two grids' cell lists, casting Bool to ℤ and summing.
2024/25.critique: The overlap test is one expression: `dup` of the '#' cell checked with `∉` against the zipped cells. It never computes column heights or separates locks from keys. Correctness assumes the cell lists line up position by position, since `zip` truncates silently and this file has no size check. Every pair is compared directly, and the operator-heavy quaalude style is hard to read without the library.

2025/1.approach: Parses lines into signed rotations (L negative, R positive); part 2 replaces each value n with `replicate (abs n) (sgn n)`. Each list gets 50 prepended, a mod-100 running sum via `scanl1`, and a `counts` lookup of 0.
2025/1.critique: `⥢` duplicates the parsed list and `⇲` maps the expansion over only the second copy, so one `both` pipeline serves both parts. Part 2 materialises every unit step, so its work grows with the summed rotation magnitudes. `counts` builds a frequency Map of all visited positions just to read key 0; `|!` returns a bare value, so missing-key behaviour depends on quaalude.

2025/2.approach: Parses comma-separated ranges and enumerates every integer in each. Digit count comes from logBase; an ID matches if repeating its leading l/s digits s times rebuilds it, and matches are summed via `Σ`.
2025/2.critique: The check is arithmetic with no string conversion. Part 2 passes [1 .. 10], and with s = 1 the check reduces to i == i, so every positive ID matches and the filter does nothing; starting the list at 2 avoids this. It is also brute force, floating-point logBase can miscount near powers of ten, and repetition counts above 10 are never tested.

2025/3.approach: For each digit line, a recursion over (index, digits remaining) either skips or takes the current digit and keeps the larger e-digit value; line results are summed for e=2 and e=12.
2025/3.critique: One function covers both parts through the digit count, and Maybe marks suffixes too short to fill the remaining digits. Recursive calls go through .$. into an MM monad keyed on the Ord (index, remaining) pair, so cost depends on that prelude machinery. The nested Maybe cases are wordy, and the quaalude operators (.$., ?, |-<..>) are hard to read without knowing the prelude.

2025/4.approach: Each round finds every '@' cell with fewer than four '@' among its eight neighbours, removes them together through grid updates, and adds up the counts. Part 1 runs one round; part 2 runs until no cell qualifies.
2025/4.critique: One `remove` with a round limit covers both parts. Passing -1 never hits the 0 case, so recursion ends only when `removable` returns empty. Every round rescans the whole grid instead of rechecking only the neighbours of removed cells. Candidates go into a set of Maybe-wrapped coordinates, which is then queried with `Just c` for each coordinate. A plain filter would be more direct.

2025/5.approach: Template Haskell embeds and parses the input into ranges and IDs. Part 1 counts IDs that fall in any range. Part 2 applies `Ŀ` with a combinator to the sorted ranges and measures the result with `|.|`.
2025/5.critique: Part 1 filters the IDs with `or` over per-range `∈` tests, costing O(ids × ranges); merging the ranges and binary-searching would avoid the full scan. Part 2 combines `(<<*>>) ∘ (max <:>)` and `(⇱) ∘ (-!) ∘ (|.|)` via `&.&` and passes this to `Ŀ` over `(fst i) 🎜`. `Ŀ` has no given signature, so how this combination behaves on the ranges cannot be determined from the code shown, and the dense point-free style makes it hard to follow.

2025/6.approach: Parses the input into number groups `ps` and operator functions `ops`. For part 2, it splits raw lines, applies `(⊤)`, cuts at all-space rows, filters digits and parses each group.
2025/6.critique: `both` runs one shared pipeline on `ps` and `psᵀ`: zip with `ops`, apply `Ŀ` via `$@`, then `!>`, then `Σ`, and combine with `<>!`. So the parts differ only in how the numbers are grouped. `<$$>` keeps the nested group structure through filtering and parsing. Readability suffers from dense, unsigned quaalude operators such as `Ŀ`, which make the core per-problem combining step opaque.

2025/7.approach: Parses a grid of 'S', '^' and '.' cells and binds the single 'S' position. A recursive function steps along increasing y from it, branching diagonally at '^' and returning a position set plus a count.
2025/7.critique: One traversal yields both answers: part 1 is the size of the returned set, part 2 the count, which adds 1 at each off-grid exit. Recursive calls go through .$. into an MM value unwrapped by run, and every '^' unions two child sets. The dense operator style is hard to read, and the refutable [s] pattern fails unless there is exactly one 'S'.

2025/8.approach: Sorts all box pairs by squared distance and merges circuits held as a Set of Sets. Part 1 applies `Ł connect` over the first 1000 pairs, then multiplies the three largest sizes. Part 2 merges until one circuit remains.
2025/8.critique: Sorting pairs once by integer squared distance (`ssd³`) avoids floating point, and that sorted list drives both parts. Each `connect` filters the circuit set twice with `(<-?-|)` to find the two endpoints' circuits, where union-find would avoid repeated searches. `final` has no empty-list case, so it is partial. The 1000 and `take 3` in `part1` are literal constants.

2025/9.approach: Parses input with `(⋮)` at type `[ℤ ⹉ 2] ≠ []`, builds `out` via `outside ∘ loopPairs` and `rects` via `triPairs`, then runs one `|-?->`, `ds²`, `🎝`, `Ȟ`, `!>` pipeline per predicate.
2025/9.critique: `<:>` applies one shared pipeline to a pair of predicates, `(⊨)` for part 1 and `not ∘ or ∘ (out <&>) ∘ (□?□)` for part 2, so the parts differ only in that predicate. In part 2 every pair produced by `triPairs` is tested with `□?□` against every element of `out`, a brute-force pairs-times-edges scan. The geometry lives in unshown helpers such as `outside` and `□?□`.

2025/10.approach: Part 1 runs a breadth-first search over string states starting from all '.', toggling characters per button, with a Set of seen states. Part 2 encodes press counts as Z3 integer variables and minimises their sum under per-counter equality constraints.
2025/10.critique: The BFS is direct but explores up to 2^n states and enqueues every successor before checking whether it was already seen, so the Seq queue grows larger than needed. Part 2 hands the integer program to Z3, which keeps it short but leaves the method opaque. Machines with no solution are silently dropped by (<>?) rather than reported.

2025/11.approach: Parses the input into a map from node names to successor lists and counts paths by recursion; part 2 recurses over (sawDac, sawFft, node) states through the `.$.` helper, unwrapped with `run`.
2025/11.critique: Carrying two flags in the state lets one recursion count only paths that visit both `dac` and `fft`. Part 1 is plain recursion with no visible caching, so shared suffixes are recomputed. Neither part tracks visited nodes, so a reachable cycle would not terminate. The Unicode operators and Template Haskell input splice keep the code short but opaque without the custom prelude.

2025/12.approach: part1 counts regions where the summed cell counts of the requested presents (count times shape size) is at most w·h; part1' instead runs a priority-queue search over placements of rotated and flipped shapes.
2025/12.critique: part1 is a single area comparison per region, linear in input size, and does not try to place any shape. part1' enumerates shape orientations with uniq and prunes states whose remaining required area exceeds free cells. Its ordering key and nested sections are very dense and hard to follow without knowing quaalude.
